The Andromeda Galaxy — 2.5 million light-years away, the most distant object visible to the naked eye. It is on a collision course with the Milky Way, arriving in about 4.5 billion years.
A compact companion of M31 whose stellar density is around a hundred times that of our own galactic bulge.
The Triangulum Galaxy — a vast, thin disc of gas and stars, the third-nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way.
The brightest galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, home to a supermassive black hole that swallows a few million solar masses a year.
The Whirlpool Galaxy — the archetype of spiral structure, its arms stirred by an ongoing encounter with companion NGC 5195.
The Sunflower Galaxy — a face-on spiral with a rich, mottled disc of young stars.
The Black Eye Galaxy — a dark band of dust crosses its disc like a smudge on an otherwise smooth face.
A near-perfect face-on spiral — one of the cleanest grand-design patterns in the sky.
Bode’s Galaxy — one of the closest and brightest spiral galaxies, and a known active nucleus.
The most luminous galaxy in the Ursa Major group; host of SN 1993J, the brightest supernova of the twentieth century.
Home of M87*, the first black hole ever imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.
The Cow's Head Galaxy, with a dense yellowish core older than most of the universe.
The Pinwheel Galaxy — a face-on disc 170,000 light-years across, lit by thousands of blue star clusters.
The Sombrero Galaxy — a brilliant bulge threaded by a razor-thin lane of dust.
A Seyfert galaxy: its core is a supermassive black hole accreting gas and shining brightly in X-rays.
The second of the two compact elliptical satellites that escort the Andromeda Galaxy.
The Sculptor Galaxy — second only to M31 among the nearest bright spirals, a starburst blowing a superwind of gas.
The classic edge-on spiral — a razor-thin disc split by a dark lane of dust.
Another razor-blade edge-on disc, one of the best in the sky for showing a galaxy’s true thinness.
One of the Mice Galaxies — two galaxies pulling on each other, stretching long tidal tails between them.
The second of the Mice pair, its tail being pulled out by its neighbour NGC 4631.
A stretched spiral in the Leo Triplet, being tidally warped by M65 and M66.
Centaurus A — a giant elliptical with a dust lane and a relativistic jet, one of the strongest radio sources in the sky.
A starburst galaxy viewed almost perfectly edge-on, its bright arm studded with young blue clusters.
A grand-design barred spiral, its arms swept out from the ends of a bright central bar.
The textbook barred spiral — the prototype for the whole SB class of galaxy.
Fornax A — a giant elliptical that has stripped its neighbours of gas and stars through collisions.
The Cigar Galaxy — a starburst furnace whose supernovae and stellar winds drive a superwind at millions of kilometres per second.
